analysis.one_liner: Applies Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes to incomes above $400,000 and funds the trust programs with it.
analysis.headline: Six Senate Democrats introduced the Medicare and Social Security Fair Share Act in May 2025; it has sat in the Senate Finance Committee ever since, with no markup, no debate, and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make earnings between today's Social Security tax cap (about $176,000 in 2025) and $400,000 subject to the 12.4% Social Security payroll tax, add a 1.2% Medicare tax on income above $400,000 ($500,000 for married couples), and extend the Medicare investment-income tax to active business profits while raising that tax to as much as 17.4% for high earners and trusts. All of the new revenue would be deposited into the Social Security and Medicare trust funds. Anyone earning under the current tax cap would pay nothing more.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security and Medicare beneficiaries, whose trust funds would receive a new, dedicated revenue stream. Workers earning under the current taxable-earnings cap would also benefit indirectly, since the programs they pay into would gain funding without any change to their own taxes.

how_it_helps.text: The bill subjects earnings between the current Social Security wage base and $400,000 to Social Security payroll taxes, for both employees and the self-employed.
It adds a further 1.2% Medicare tax on wages and self-employment income above $400,000, or above $500,000 on a joint return.

It extends the 3.8% net investment income tax to active business profits that high-income owners currently shield from it, and raises the rate applied to undistributed income of trusts and estates to 17.4%.

The bill routes the new revenue to the trust funds, directing 28.7% of the investment-income tax to Medicare's Hospital Insurance fund and the remainder to Social Security's old-age, survivors, and disability funds.

analysis.who_pays: Individuals with wage or self-employment income above $400,000 ($500,000 for couples), owners of businesses taxed as pass-throughs (partnerships, S corporations, and LLCs) whose operating profits would newly face the Medicare investment-income tax, and high-income trusts and estates.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners and pass-through business owners

drawbacks.text: The bill raises payroll taxes on income up to $400,000 without changing the Social Security benefit formula, so top earners would pay more in Social Security tax without a proportional increase in their own benefits.

Taxes would rise steeply just above the $400,000 and $500,000 thresholds, creating sharp jumps in marginal rates that opponents argue discourage additional work and business investment near those lines.

Owners of pass-through businesses — partnerships, S corporations, and LLCs — would face materially higher taxes because their active business income would no longer be exempt from the net investment income tax, a cost small and mid-sized business owners say falls on them rather than only on the very wealthy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would put a new, dedicated funding stream behind the two largest retirement and health programs, at a cost borne entirely by households and business owners above $400,000 in income. The main honest objections are that the thresholds create steep rate cliffs, that top earners pay more without added benefits, and that the expanded tax on 'specified net income' adds real complexity for business owners below billionaire level. On the whole, the gains accrue broadly to tens of millions of beneficiaries while the costs are concentrated at the top.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on May 8, 2025, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has remained with no further action.

narrative.text: Senator Whitehouse introduced the bill on May 8, 2025, joined by Senators Klobuchar and Van Hollen, and it drew 5 Democratic cosponsors.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance on May 8, 2025.
The Finance Committee has taken no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners and pass-through business owners who would have paid the new taxes are better off, because the bill never left committee and no tax has changed.

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Finance Committee.

against.name: Sen. Mike Crapo
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a markup or vote since the bill was referred to his committee.

against.name: Sen. John Thune
against.what_they_did: Has not brought the bill to the Senate floor for debate or a vote.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor is a Democrat (6 of 45 Senate Democrats), and the Republican majority that controls the Finance Committee and the floor calendar has taken no action on it.

industries.note: They would face Social Security payroll taxes on income between the current cap and $400,000 plus a new 1.2% Medicare surtax above that level, while workers under the cap pay nothing more. Their gain from the bill stalling is the trust funds' lost revenue.

industries.industry: Pass-through business owners (partnerships, S corporations, LLCs)
industries.note: Active business profits are currently exempt from the 3.8% net investment income tax; the bill would pull them back in, plus a 13.6% additional bracket for high earners. Business owners have a direct financial interest in keeping the bill off the floor.
Carried interest and partnership income would count as taxable investment income under the expanded rules, sharply raising taxes on fund managers' main income source.
The tax on undistributed investment income of trusts and estates would jump from 3.8% to 17.4%, a major cost for families using trusts to hold and pass on wealth.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding 55 of 100 Senate seats and the chairmanship of the Finance Committee, the bill is very unlikely to receive a markup or a floor vote this Congress. Comparable payroll-tax extension proposals from Democratic senators in recent Congresses also died in committee without a vote.
